sections.h2: What should you know before selling a house in Upper Arlington, Ohio?
sections.html:
Upper Arlington is a planned suburb on the northwest side of Columbus, and a sale there turns on lot layout, school boundaries and a handful of city rules that older houses trigger. The city sits in Franklin County between the Scioto River on the west and Columbus on the north and east. The Census Bureau lists its land area at 9.79 square miles.

Census estimates show 35,893 residents on July 1, 2025, down from the 36,800 counted in the 2020 census. The sections below cover what the city checks, what Franklin County handles and what Ohio asks of a seller on paper, so you can decide how fast a sale can realistically move.

sections.h2: How did Upper Arlington's planned layout shape its houses?
sections.html:
Two brothers who developed real estate bought the first 840 acres south of present-day Lane Avenue in 1913 and followed a Garden City plan with deep setbacks, parks and separate zones for shops and apartments. The place was called the Country Club District at first and carried the Upper Arlington name by 1917. It incorporated as a village in 1918 and became a city on February 8, 1941.

Annexation did the rest. Most of it came between the late 1940s and 1960, and the two largest, in 1954 and 1955, nearly doubled the city's area. Henderson Road has marked the northern edge since 1969. The result is two housing stocks on one map:

  • South of Lane Avenue, the Old Arlington district holds Colonial and English Revival houses. The district went onto the National Register of Historic Places in 1985.
  • North of Lane, post-war tracts such as River Ridge follow ordinary street grids with ranch houses, and the houses built from the 1960s on grew larger.

Which side of Lane Avenue your house sits on decides which city rules you run into first.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about owning in Upper Arlington?
sections.html:
Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 describe a high-value, owner-heavy suburb. A buyer shopping here compares your house against a high-priced local market, so condition and presentation carry weight.

  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 79.4%.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $595,600.
  • Median monthly owner costs: $3,189 with a mortgage and $1,284 without one.
  • Households: 14,330, at 2.52 people per household.
  • Median household income: $155,167; 79.8% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher.
  • Residents living in the same house a year earlier: 88.2%.

Mean travel time to work is 19.3 minutes, which fits a suburb a short drive from downtown Columbus and from the Ohio State campus east of the Olentangy River. The Upper Arlington City School District serves the whole city, and its high school was rebuilt in 2021.

sections.h2: Does the Old Arlington demolition rule affect a sale?
sections.html:
It can, if the buyer plans to tear the house down. In 2009 City Council adopted rules meant to discourage, without prohibiting, total demolition of historically significant homes. A six-month delay period gives owners and the city time to look for alternatives, and the rules appear in Articles 5, 6 and 7 of the Unified Development Ordinance.

The city's GIS maps show which properties are identified as historically significant, and Community Development posts a Guide to Demolition in the Historic District along with an owner statement and a demolition sign affidavit. If you are selling a house south of Lane Avenue to a builder or investor, tell the buyer up front and ask Community Development whether your parcel is flagged.

sections.h2: Which city offices handle permits and exterior complaints?
sections.html:
Community Development covers three divisions: Planning, Building and Code Compliance. Its office is at 3600 Tremont Road and is open Monday through Friday from 8 am to 5 pm. The main line is 614-583-5070 and inspections are scheduled at 614-583-5080.

Exterior upkeep is mostly complaint driven. The city lists high grass and weeds, flaking paint, illegal temporary signs, excess lighting, trash and debris, and noise as common violations. A written Notice of Violation follows a confirmed complaint and sets a re-inspection date, which an officer may extend for substantial progress, bad weather or other mitigating circumstances. Most violations carry a maximum of $150 per offense per day, and a few are fourth degree misdemeanors with a $250 maximum fine and up to 30 days in jail.

sections.h2: What can you do with a cluttered or dated house before listing?
sections.html:
The city's own pages answer the practical questions. Bulk items go to the curb by 7 am on your regular collection day, and mattresses and box springs must be wrapped in plastic. Large appliances and anything containing Freon may cost extra, so ask Local Waste Services at 614-409-9375, option 2, before you set them out.

  • One garage or yard sale per residence is allowed in any six-month period, for no more than three consecutive days, with no permit.
  • A plumbing permit is needed to install or replace a boiler, water heater or water meter, or any time supply or waste lines change.
  • Decks, fences, driveway replacements, detached garages and pools each appear as their own permit type in the online system.

Finished basements, new decks and swapped water heaters are the usual places a permit gap shows up. Pull the permit history first and close any gap before you accept an offer.

sections.h2: How do rental registration and the value complaint work in Franklin County?
sections.html:
Upper Arlington lies wholly inside Franklin County, so the county auditor handles both. Under Ohio Revised Code 5323.02 an owner of residential rental property must file contact information with the auditor. The filing is due within 60 days after the notice that follows a transfer or the arrival of a tax bill, and each property that stays unfiled faces a $150 fine per tax year. Out-of-state owners must name an in-state contact.

A value complaint goes to the same auditor. Under ORC 5715.19 it must be filed by March 31 of the following year or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later. The 2025 tax year window closed March 31, 2026. The board hears the property's value, and the tax bill itself is outside its scope.

Franklin County's standard Homestead Exemption goes to owners 65 or older as of December 31 of the application year, or permanently and totally disabled, under an income limit. A separate enhanced exemption for veterans rated 100% disabled covers taxes owed on $50,000 of appraised value with no income test.

sections.h2: What must an Ohio seller hand to the buyer?
sections.html:
Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 requires the seller of a one-to-four unit home to fill out the state disclosure form and deliver a signed, dated copy as soon as practicable. A buyer who gets the form only after signing a contract may rescind within three business days of receiving it, and a buyer who never receives it may rescind within the earlier of 30 days after acceptance or closing.

Fill the form out honestly and update it if something changes. The statute lets a seller make a good faith approximation of an item they truly do not know.

sections.h2: How do you compare ways to sell quickly in Upper Arlington?
sections.html:
The comparison comes down to time against price. A listing with an agent exposes the house to owner-occupant buyers, which takes showings and a buyer's financing timeline. A direct buyer who purchases as-is can shorten that timeline, and the offer reflects the repairs the buyer takes on.

  • Ask every buyer to put in writing who pays closing costs, how many days to closing and whether repairs are excluded.
  • Ask for proof of funds before you sign anything.
  • Check the permit history and any open exterior complaint before you list, because both affect timing.

faqs.q: Does Upper Arlington require a permit for a deck or fence?
faqs.a: Yes, both appear as residential permit types in the city's online permit system. Call Community Development at 614-583-5070 before work starts, and check that earlier work on your house has a closed permit.

faqs.q: Can a buyer tear down my Old Arlington house?
faqs.a: Often yes, after a delay. The 2009 rules in the Unified Development Ordinance set a six-month delay period for total demolition of historically significant homes. Ask Community Development whether your parcel is identified in the city's GIS maps.

faqs.q: Do I need to register a rental house in Upper Arlington before selling it?
faqs.a: Registration is a Franklin County Auditor requirement under Ohio Revised Code 5323.02. An unregistered property faces a $150 fine per tax year, so file or update the contact record before closing. The auditor's line is 614-525-4663.

faqs.q: When can I dispute my home's value?
faqs.a: File with the Franklin County Auditor by March 31 of the year after the tax year, or the first-half collection deadline if it falls later. The Board of Revision, at 614-525-3913, decides value only.

faqs.q: Who completes the Ohio property disclosure form?
faqs.a: The seller does. Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 requires the form for most one-to-four unit sales, and certain transfers, such as those between co-owners or to a spouse or a lineal relative, are exempt.
